gloss: cf. the Collect, “We pray thee that thy grace may always prevent and follow us.”
an allusion to Romans viii. 26, “the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered.”
*yet*; referring back to line 1—‘though they were in lowly plight, yet was their demeanour not mean.’ *port*, bearing.

The Greek story of Deucalion and Pyrrha corresponds to the Scriptural account of the Flood. They were the only survivors from the Deluge, and they consulted the sanctuary of Themis, goddess of custom and equity, how the race of man should be restored. Ovid tells the tale, *Metamorphoses* I. 260 et seq., and M. is thinking of his version.
tending, cultivating.
meeting. The word has retained its ecclesiastical associations.

the Biblical references are to the giving of the ten commandments to Moses on Sinai, Exod. xix. 16–19, and to “the last trump,” mentioned in the New Testament, e.g. in 1 Cor. xv. 52. M. qualifies (“perhaps”) his suggestion that the trumpet may be the same.

the amaranth is a type of immortality, and therefore placed by M. in Heaven. See the fine passage in III. 353–59, where he tells us that this flower once flourished in Eden “by the tree of life,” and then, after man’s offence, “to Heaven removed.”
forbidden.

Michael had not yet been chosen for the discharge of any duty in the action of the poem, as had Gabriel (bk. IV.) and Raphael (bk. V.). But he had been mentioned in bk. VI. as playing a great part in the battle in Heaven.
pity; in Shakespeare the usual sense is ‘pity, tenderness of heart.’ *denounce*, announce, proclaim, with the notion of hostility or menace.
*double*, because the Latin divinity Janus was commonly represented with two faces. Janus sometimes appears as *quadrifrons*, i.e. with four faces.
Argus, the hundred-eyed monster who was set by Hera (Juno) to watch over Io; some of his eyes watched while the others rested. Hermes (Mercury) soothed him to sleep with music, and killed him.
his wand or caduceus, made of olive-wood and entwined with two serpents, which conferred sleep on whomsoever he wished.

the Greek Leucothea, the white or bright goddess, was identified by the Romans with their deity Matuta or Mater Matuta, the goddess of the dawn. Lucretius, V. 655, speaks of Matuta ushering in the dawn; this office M. transfers to Leucothea.
alluding to Gen. iii. 20, “And Adam called his wife’s name Eve; because she was the mother of all living.” The name is said to mean ‘life.’
agreed, assented; the metaphor of signing a document.
here the omens are symbolical: the two birds and two beasts represent the human pair; and the direction of their flight—“to the eastern gate”—foreshadows the banishment from Eden.

“The severe censure on this makes me fancy that Milton hinted at the war with Holland, which broke out in 1664, when we surprised and took the Dutch Bourdeaux fleet, before war was proclaim’d” (Warburton).

Raphael is called “the sociable Spirit” in V. 221. “Among the angels, the virtue of Raphael is mild and placid, of easy condescension and free communication; that of Michael is regal and lofty” (Johnson).
Iris was the classical goddess of the rainbow, and the verse is a poetical way of saying that the vest was brilliant as with the hues of a rainbow.
i.e. disappointed of his prey for many days (*seizure* being passive). Keightley noted that the language of the lines is mainly legal.
“for she had commenced her existence in Paradise” (Keightley); whereas Adam, created elsewhere, was placed in Eden.
depression of spirits.
the verb *can*, ‘to know how to,’ i.e. ‘to be able,’ was not then, as now, a mere auxiliary.
for Adam the altars would serve as actual reminders (in memory), for his descendants as memorials: it is the distinction between personal experience and historical tradition.

lemma: To show thee what shall come
gloss: the whole idea of the vision was probably suggested to Milton by the vision of his descendants vouchsafed to Aeneas. Addison had noted that the “vision” in bks. XI., XII. is designed to modify the feeling of Adam’s failure which the close of the poem leaves.
cf. Ezekiel xl. 2, “In the visions of God brought he me into the land of Israel, and set me upon a very high mountain.” The phrase means ‘visions sent by God.’
strictly Cathay was identical with China, and Cambaluc, its capital, was the same as Pekin. Cambaluc, built by Kublai Khan, was the capital of the Mongol Emperors of China, from about 1264 to 1368.

lemma: Agra and Lahor of great Mogul
gloss: these names represent India, Lahore being in the Punjaub while Agra is the capital of the N.W. provinces. *Mogul*=Arabic *Mughal*=Mongol.

*Ispahan*, or *Isfahan*, became the capital of Persia in the reign of the Shah Abbas the Great, who ruled 1586–1628. *Ksar* is a corruption of Lat. *Caesar*; hence identical with Germ. *Kaiser*. *Bizance*=Byzantium, Constantinople.

the empire meant is Upper Ethiopia or Abyssinia; *Negus*, ‘king,’ was the hereditary title of the monarch of the country. *Ercoco*, now generally spelt Arkeeko, is a port on the Red Sea, at the northernmost (i.e. “utmost”) point of Abyssinia.

*Sofala*; on the same coast, but further south. *Ophir*; whence Solomon’s fleet brought gold and precious stones, 1 Kings ix. 28, x. 11. According to Genesis x. 29, 30, Ophir was in southern Arabia, and not on the east side of Africa.

*Cusco*, i.e. Cuzco, in the centre of Peru; it was formerly the capital of the empire of the Incas, whose last native sovereign, Atahuallpa—in the Spanish form, Atabalipa—was conquered by the Spaniard, Pizarro, 1532–33.

lemma: Guiana, whose great city Geryon’s sons
gloss: in the 16th and 17th centuries a popular belief obtained that in the north-east of South America there existed a region of fabulous wealth, termed by the Spanish El Dorado, ‘the Golden.’ *Geryon’s sons*, the Spanish; Geryon being the Spanish king whose oxen Hercules carried off.

the plant ‘eye-bright.’ According to the old doctrine of the Signatures, the efficacy of a plant was indicated by its similarity in colour or shape to the part of the body diseased: euphrasy has a flower with an eye-like mark: hence its use as a remedy for dim sight.
cf. III. 51–55, where M. contrasts the light of the eyes with that of the soul. The blind Samson was “with inward eyes illuminated,” *S. A.* 1689.
The story of Cain and Abel, Genesis iv.
Gen. iv. 4 only says, “And the Lord had respect unto Abel and to his offering”; but the verse is usually explained as M. has interpreted it.

This notion of the “cave” of Death, crowded with personified shapes of evil and disease, is purely conventional: many such pictures have been painted by poets. We may remember that the fourth draft of *Paradise Lost* contained “a mask of all the evils of this world.”
a hospital for lepers, *lazar* coming from the name of the beggar in Luke xvi. 20.
the couplet, as editors note, is made up of reminiscences of Shakespeare. Cf. *Macbeth*, V. 8. 31, “And thou opposed, being of no woman born.”

alluding to the maxim of the ancients, *ne quid nimis*. The praises of a temperate life are often on Milton’s lips. No doubt, in the present passage, M. is thinking of his own habits. A “temperate man,” says Aubrey.
M. is probably glancing at his own ill-health in later life. “He died of the gowt struck in” (Aubrey). Aubrey says that he bore his suffering very cheerfully.

Referring to the descendants of Cain; see Gen. iv. 20–22. In 560 “who moved” means Jubal, “the father of all such as handle the harp and organ,” Gen. iv. 21. The organ was Milton’s favourite instrument; he had been taught to play it by his father.

*transverse*, across, i.e. across the keys of the instrument. A *fugue* (Ital. *fuga*, ‘a flight’) is a form of musical composition. The whole passage has often been cited as a striking instance of Milton’s accuracy in the use of technical terms of music.

lemma: But on the hither side, a different sort
gloss: referring to the descendants of Seth. According to Jewish tradition they dwelt in the mountains near to Paradise (i.e. “on the hither side”), whereas Cain went out to “the east of Eden,” Gen. iv. 16. They are said by Josephus to have been addicted to the study of physics and astronomy.
the classical god of marriage. The colouring here (590–92) is classical.

*troll*, properly ‘to roll’; but commonly *troll* was used in phrases like ‘troll a catch’ (in music). The notion there is ‘to run over glibly, fluently.’ Probably, therefore, M. means that these “goddesses” are voluble of speech.
“The sons of God saw the daughters of men that they were fair,” Gen. vi. 2. “It is now generally agreed, that this passage is to be understood of the sons of Seth” (Newton).

an expression of Milton’s own opinion. Unhappy in his first marriage, which led to the composition of his bitter pamphlets on Divorce, and in the ill-behaviour of his daughters, he seldom let pass an opportunity for invective against women. There is probably a quibble here, an old derivation of *woman* being *woe to man*!

Obviously modelled on the description of the shield of Achilles, *Iliad* XVIII. 478 et seq. Cf. the use that Vergil makes of the same passage in *Aeneid* VIII. 608–731, describing the shield which Venus brings to Aeneas.
i.e. Enoch, of middle age; Enoch was 365 years old when translated to Heaven—“i.e. not half the full age attributed to the oldest patriarchs” (Masson).
“This was probably intended by the poet as a reflection on the dangerous doctrine of his antagonist, Hobbes; who wished to establish the false notion, that right is founded on might” (Todd).
Milton’s own “ill-mated” first marriage had strongly influenced his life and opinions.

lemma: Rapt in a balmy cloud with winged steeds
gloss: he assumes that Enoch’s translation to Heaven resembled that of Elijah (2 Kings ii. 11).
a much stronger word then than now. In Shakespeare it always means ‘lust, lasciviousness.’

Genesis vi., vii. There are occasional echoes in the passage of Ovid’s description of the Deluge (*Metamorphoses* I.); e.g. “sea without shore” in 750 suggests Ovid’s *deerant quoque litora ponto*, I. 292.
Matthew vi. 34, “Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.” *dispensed*, i.e. distributed so as to be the burden.

lemma: with their freedom lost, all virtue lose
gloss: Milton’s favourite idea, that in the history of every nation moral corruption and loss of political liberty go hand in hand: that a people which is corrupt ceases to care for freedom. The thought is often insisted upon in his prose-works.

a picture of Milton himself in the lonely last years of his life; perhaps he meant it as such. The “dark age” represented that in which the Restoration had been brought about; the “wicked ways” were those of the courtiers of Charles II.
in Gen. vii. 11, the Heb. word rendered by *windows* in the A.V. is translated *cataracts* in the Vulgate. The word is appropriate of tropical rain and water-spouts.
it was a generally held opinion that Paradise was obliterated by the Flood; but the particular explanation here given of its removal appears to be of Milton’s own invention.
“And God made a wind to pass over the earth, and the waters asswaged,” Gen. viii. 1. M. would naturally select the north as the parching, drying wind.
*three*, red, yellow and blue (according to the belief then held). Now the rainbow is resolved into seven colours. *listed*, striped, streaked; from *list*, a strip (of cloth, etc.).

lemma: as the brow of God appeased
gloss: the notion is that of a knitted brow relaxing its wrinkled lines, i.e. the frown, expressive of anger or thought.
